newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to give TV appeal in bid to regain momentum.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to give TV appeal in bid to regain momentum.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac was to give a rare television interview on Thursday in a bid to restore confidence in his embattled conservative government but opposition leaders dismissed it as a public relations stunt.
Aides ruled out the announcement of a change of government or abrupt policy changes during the prime-time 90-minute broadcast beginning at 8.50 p.m. (1950 GMT).
Instead, they said Chirac hoped to win over sceptics by better explaining the long-term benefits of his austerity policies on the eve of a key European Union summit in Dublin.

French media noted that Chirac had hinted on Monday there could be "a surprise" in the broadcast. But most discounted talk of a major initiative such as a cabinet reshuffle, a referendum or a dissolution of parliament to hold a general election early next year, a full year ahead of schedule.

Chirac's aides chose the forum -- an elegant Elysee palace room -- and the five young, relatively inexperienced journalists who would question him, saying they hoped to avoid a boring and predictable political interview programme.
But some critics charged that veteran political journalists had been excluded to assure that Chirac would be pitched only softball questions.

"The president is hoping for a public relations coup, but this is no time for show business," said Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande. "The French people want to hear a message about more economic growth, greater purchasing power and maybe some perspectives on the future."

Chirac and his Prime Minister Alain Juppe have seen their popularity ratings slump to rock-bottom levels in recent polls over record unemployment, sluggish economic growth, simmering labour unrest and corruption scandals in their Gaullist party.

The government has also been shaken by problems with its plan to privatise defence and consumer electronics group Thomson SA, and by a renewed danger from suspected Algerian Islamic bombers and Corsican separatists.
A CSA opinion poll released on Wednesday found that 54 percent of French voters want Juppe out as prime minister.
"I am struck by how quickly he (Chirac) has lost his credibility and his power. His seven-year term has just begun," Socialist official Henri Emmanuelli said on Europe 1 radio.

Chirac took office in mid-May 1995. His woes began soon afterwards when he jettisoned campaign promises to create jobs, raise salaries and heal France's social fracture and turned to public spending cuts and tax increases to help Paris qualify for European monetary union from 1999.

With a general election due in March 1998 and polls showing gains on both the left and the far-right at the expense of the ruling centre-right coalition, government back-benchers have taken to open sniping against Juppe's policies.

One option could be for Chirac to call early parliamentary elections in the hope the centre-right would be returned to power for the remaining five years of his presidential term, albeit with a greatly reduced majority, political sources said.
But the president, who has the constitutional right to dissolve parliament once a year, has dismissed such a move in the past, saying it would only be legitimate if there were a political crisis.
The centre-right coalition holds 480 of the 577 National Assembly seats and, despite bickering, has never denied the government its support.
The president has repeatedly ruled out dumping Juppe, saying the premier is implementing necessary policies with courage.
Chirac's TV appearance marked the first time he had addressed the nation since July 14 apart from a brief statement vowing to fight terrorism after last week's Paris metro bomb.
